0. Overview of the lecture¶

  • We discuss multivariate time series modeling in this lecture.
  • We first study multivariate generalizations of ACF and Ljung-Box test.
  • We then learn about VAR(p) models which are the multivariate extension of univariate AR models and are among the simplest and most commonly used multivariate time series model.

1. Multivariate times series¶

  • Consider a $k$ dimensional time series $\{\rv_t\} = \{(r_{t,1}, \dots, r_{t,k})^\top\}$.
  • So far, we have only consider temporal dependence (i.e. dependence across time) for univariate time series
  • In ARIMAX, we had two time series. However, we did not consider dependence of $Y_t$ on $X_{t-1}$. We only consider dependence of $Y_t$ on $X_t$
  • We now turn our attention to studying multivariate time series.
  • Multivariate time series models are, in general, much more complicated that univariate models, especially as the dimension of the time series increases.

1.1. Stationary time series¶

  • As in the univariate case, we start by introducing the notion of stationarity
  • Strict stationary: $\{\rv_t\}$ is strictly stationary if its finite dimensional distributions are time invariant. In other words, for any integers $m$, $t_1<t_2<\ldots<t_m$, and $T$, the joint distribution of \begin{align*} (\rv_{t_1}, \rv_{t_2}, \dots, \rv_{t_m}) \end{align*} and \begin{align*} (\rv_{t_1+T}, \rv_{t_2+T}, \dots, \rv_{t_m+T}) \end{align*} is the same.
  • Weak stationarity: For $\{\rv_t\}$, define the first two moments as follows \begin{align*} \muv(t) = \Eb(\rv_t),\quad\text{ and }\qquad \Gamv(t,h) = \Cov(\rv_t, \rv_{t-h}). \end{align*} $\{\rv_t\}$ is weakly stationary if $\muv(t)$ and $\Gamv(t,h)$ exist and are $t$ invariant. That is, there exist a constant vector $\muv$ and a matrix function $\Gamv(h)$ such that \begin{align*} \muv(t)=\muv,\quad\text{ and }\quad \Gamv(t,h)=\Gamv(h), \end{align*} for all $t$.

1.2. Moments of (weakly) stationary time series¶

  • Let $\{\rv_t\}$ be (weakly) stationary.
  • The mean of $\{\rv_t\}$ is $\muv:=\Eb(\rv_t)$
  • The covariance matrix of $\{\rv_t\}$ is $\Gamv_0:=\Eb\left((\rv_t-\muv)(\rv_t-\muv)^\top\right)$. Clearly, $\Gamv_0$ is symmetric. We also assume that it is of full rank. So, we assume that $\Gam_0$ is positive definite.
  • What if $\Gamv_0$ is not of full rank?
  • Then at least one element of $\rv_t$ can be written as a linear combination of the rest. So, we can reduce the dimension of $\{\rv_t\}$
  • The lag-$h$ autocovariance matrix of $\{\rv_t\}$ is $\Gamv_h := \Eb\left((\rv_t-\muv)(\rv_{t-h}-\muv)^\top\right)$
  • Note, however, that the autocovariance matrix is NOT symmetric!
  • To see this, let us consider a stationary bivariate time series $\{\rv_t\}=\{(r_{t,1}, r_{t,2})^\top\}$
  • We have
\begin{align*} \Gamv_h &= \Eb\left((\rv_t-\muv)(\rv_{t-h}-\muv)^\top\right)\\\\ &=\Eb\left(\begin{pmatrix}r_{t,1}-\mu_1\\ r_{t,2}-\mu_2\end{pmatrix}(r_{t-h,1}-\mu_1, r_{t-h,2}-\mu_2)\right)\\\\ &=\begin{pmatrix}\Eb\left(r_{t,1}-\mu_1)(r_{t-h,1}-\mu_1)\right) & \Eb\left(r_{t,1}-\mu_1)(r_{t-h,2}-\mu_2)\right)\\ \Eb\left(r_{t,2}-\mu_2)(r_{t-h,1}-\mu_1)\right) & \Eb\left(r_{t,2}-\mu_2)(r_{t-h,2}-\mu_2)\right)\end{pmatrix}\\\\ &=\begin{pmatrix}\Cov(r_{t,1}, r_{t-h,1}) & \Cov(r_{t,1}, r_{t-h,2})\\ \Cov(r_{t,2}, r_{t-h,1}) & \Cov(r_{t,2}, r_{t-h,2})\end{pmatrix} \end{align*}
  • In general, $\Gamv_{h,ij} =$ $ \Cov(r_{t,i},$ $ r_{t-h,j})$
  • Note that $\Gamv_{h,ij} =$ $ \Cov$ $(r_{t,i},$ $ r_{t-h,j})$ $ \ne $ $\Cov$ $(r_{t,j}, $ $r_{t-h,i}$ $) =$ $ \Gamv_{h,ji}$
  • Note, however, that
\begin{align*} \Gamv_{-h,ij} &= \Cov(r_{t,i}, r_{t-(-h),j}) \\ & = \Cov(r_{t+h,j}, r_{t,i})\\ & = \Cov(r_{t,j}, r_{t-h,i})\quad\quad \text{ by stationarity}\\ & = \Gam_{-h,ji} \end{align*}
  • Thus, $\Gamv_{-h} $ $= $ $\Gamv_h^\top$
  • The diagonal elements of $\Gamv_h$ are $\Cov(r_{t,i}, r_{t-h,i})$. These are the lag-h autocovariance terms of the univariate time series $\{r_{t,i}\}$, $i=1,\dots,k$.
  • The off-diagonal elements of $\Gamv_h$ are $\Cov(r_{t,i}, r_{t-h,j})$ for $i\ne j$. These are the cross-covariance between $\{r_{t,i}\}$ and $\{r_{t,j}\}$.
  • To distinguish the non-symmetric aspect of $\Gamv_h$, it is usually called the cross-covariance matrix.
  • Let $\sig_i$ be the standard deviation of $r_{t,i}$. These are the square root of diagonal elements of $\Gamv_0$.
  • Define $\Dv$ $=$ $\diag($ $\sig_1,$ $\dots,$ $\sig_k)$.
  • The correlation matrix of $\{\rv_t\}$ is \begin{align*} \rhov_0 = \Dv^{-1}\Gamv_0\Dv^{-1} \end{align*}
  • The lag-h cross-correlation matrix (CCM) of $\{\rv_t\}$ is \begin{align*} \rhov_h = \Dv^{-1}\Gamv_h\Dv^{-1} \end{align*}
  • This is the normalized version of the cross-covariance matrix, and is a generalization of the univariate auto-correlation function (ACF). $\rhov_h$ is also called the cross-correlation function (CCF)
  • $\rho_{h,ij}$ is the correlation between $r_{t,i}$ and $r_{t-h,j}$, while $\rho_{h,ji}$ is the correlation between $r_{t,j}$ and $r_{t-h,i}$. So, $\rhov_h$, $h>0$, is not symmetric.
  • We have $\rhov_{-h}$ $=$ $\rhov_h^\top$

1.3. Sample CCM (or CCF)¶

  • Next, we consider estimating the first two moments of a stationary multivariate time series.
  • Assume that we are given a time series $\{\rv_1,\dots, \rv_T\}$.
  • The sample mean, which estimates $\muv=\Eb(\rv_t)$, is given by \begin{align*} \widehat{\muv} = \overline{\rv} := \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T \rv_t. \end{align*}
  • The sample covariance matrix, which estimates $\Gamv_0=\Cov(\rv_t)$, is given by \begin{align*} \widehat{\Gamv}_0 := \frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{t=1}^T (\rv_t-\widehat{\muv})(\rv_t-\widehat{\muv})^\top. \end{align*}
  • The lag-"h" sample cross-covariance, which estimates $\Gamv_h=\Cov(\rv_t, \rv_{t-h})$, is given by \begin{align*} \widehat{\Gamv}_h := \frac{1}{T-h-1}\sum_{t=h+1}^T (\rv_t-\widehat{\muv})(\rv_{t-h}-\widehat{\muv})^\top. \end{align*}
  • Finally, the lag-"h" sample CCM (or CCF), which estimates $\rhov_h=\Corr(\rv_t, \rv_{t-h})$, is given by \begin{align*} \widehat{\rhov}_h := \widehat{\Dv}^{-1}\widehat{\Gamv}_h\widehat{\Dv}^{-1},\\ ~ \end{align*} where $\widehat{\Dv}=\diag(\sqrt{\widehat{\Gamv}_{0,11}},\dots, \sqrt{\widehat{\Gamv}_{0,kk}})$ is the diagonal matrix of sample standard deviations of $\{r_{t,1},\dots,r_{t,k}\}$.

1.4. Multivariate Ljung-Box test¶

  • Similar to the univariate case, we will need to check if cross-correlation is zero or not.
  • The are two types of tests
  • Individual tests: $H_0: \rhov_h=0$ versus $H_1: \rhov_l\ne 0$
  • Note that the "individual tests" involves multiple parameters. So, they are a joint test!
  • We refer to them as "individual" tests because they test an individual lag
  • The test statistic is $C_h = T $ $\vec(\widehat{\rhov}_h)^\top$ $ (\widehat{\rhov}_0^{-1}$ $\otimes$ $\widehat{\rhov}_0^{-1})$ $ \vec(\widehat{\rhov}_h)$
  • Under $H_0$ and the additional assumption that $\rv_1,\dots,\rv_T$ are jointly normal,, then $C_h$ is asymptotically chi-squared with $k^2$ degrees of freedom.
  • Let $\Av=[\av_1,\dots, \av_n]$ be an $m\times n$ matrix with columns $\av_1,\dots, \av_n$
  • We define the stacking operator as $\vec(\Av) = \begin{pmatrix} \av_1\\ \vdots \\ \av_n\end{pmatrix}$. That is, we stack columns of $\Av$ to form a $mn\times 1$ vector.
  • Example:
\begin{align*} \vec\left(\left[\begin{array}{c c} 2 & 1\\ -1 & 3\end{array}\right]\right) = \begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\1\\3\end{pmatrix} \end{align*}
  • Let $\Av_{m\times n}$ and $\Bv_{\ell\times k}$ be two matrices
  • The Kronecker product is an $m\ell\times nk$ matrix given by \begin{align*} \Av\otimes\Bv = \begin{bmatrix} a_{11}\Bv & a_{12} \Bv & \dots & a_{1n}\Bv\\ a_{21}\Bv & a_{22} \Bv & \dots & a_{2n}\Bv\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ a_{m1}\Bv & a_{m2} \Bv & \dots & a_{mn}\Bv \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}
  • Example: \begin{align*} \left[\begin{array}{c c} 2 & 1\\ -1 & 3\end{array}\right]\otimes \left[\begin{array}{c c} 4 & -1 & 3\\ -2 & 5 & 2\end{array}\right] = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & -2 & 6 & 4 &-1 &3\\ -4 &10 &4 &-2 &5 &2\\-4& 1& -3 &12& -3& 9\\ 2 &-5& -2 &-6 &15 &6\end{bmatrix} \end{align*}
  • Consider, again, the weekly rate changes of 1-year and 3-year treasury rates.
In [3]:
library(quantmod)
getSymbols(c("WGS1YR","WGS3YR"), src="FRED", auto.assign=TRUE)
ydiff = diff(na.locf(merge(WGS1YR,WGS3YR))[index(WGS1YR)])
names(ydiff)=c('c1','c3')
c1= na.omit(as.numeric(ydiff$c1));c3=na.omit(as.numeric(ydiff$c3));
par(mfrow=c(1,2));par(mar=c(4,4,4,4))
plot(ydiff, legend.loc='topright', major.ticks = "years",
     grid.ticks.on = "years", grid.col = "lightgray")
plot(c1,c3,xlab="c1", ylab="c3")
  1. 'WGS1YR'
  2. 'WGS3YR'
  • To get the sample cross correlation between any two univariate time series, use R base function ccf()
  • Note that $\rho_{h,21}=\rho_{-h,12}$. So, we can show $\rho_{h,12}$ and $\rho_{h,21}$ in one plot!
  • The individual test can be performed as in a sample ACF plot. There seems to be significant cross correlation in the bivariate time series.
In [4]:
ccf(c1,c3)
  • What do the values of CCF indicate?
  • Positive lags are correlation of $c1$ and lagged values of $c3$. Negative lags are correlation of $c3$ and lagged values of $c1$.
  • If one passes a multivariate time series to acf() function, it returns the sample CCM.
  • Compare the information to the CCF plot.
In [5]:
acf(coredata(na.omit(ydiff)))
  • Joint tests: $H_0: \rhov_1=\dots=\rhov_m=0$ versus $H_1:$ $\rhov_h\ne 0$ for at least one $h\in\{1,\dots,m\}$
  • We refer to them as "joint" tests because they test multiple lags simultaneously.
  • The test is the multivariate generalization of the Ljung-Box test, and is referred to as the multivariate Ljung-Box test. It is also called the multivariate Portmanteau test.
  • The test statistic is \begin{align*} Q_k(m) := \sum_{h=1}^m \frac{T}{T-h} C_h = T^2 \sum_{h=1}^m \frac{1}{T-h}\vec(\widehat{\rhov}_h)^\top (\widehat{\rhov}_0^{-1}\otimes\widehat{\rhov}_0^{-1}) \vec(\widehat{\rhov}_h). \end{align*}
  • Under $H_0$ and the additional assumption that $\rv_1,\dots,\rv_T$ are jointly normal, the test statistic $Q_k(m)$ is asymptotically chi-squared with $k^2$ degrees of freedom.
  • To perform a multivariate Ljung-Box test, we can use the mq() function of the MTS package.
In [7]:
library(MTS)
mq(coredata(na.omit(ydiff)), lag = 5)

2. Vector autoregressive (VAR) model¶

  • A $k$ dimensional time series $\{\rv_t = (r_{t,1}, \dots, r_{t,k})^\top\}_{t=1}^T$ has a VAR(p) model if
\begin{align*} \begin{cases} \rv_t - \muv = \sum_{i=1}^p \Phi_i (\rv_{t-i}-\muv) + \av_t\\\\ \av_t \sim \text{weak WN}(\0_{k\times 1},\Sig_{k\times k}) \end{cases} \end{align*}
  • The VAR(p) equation can be written as follows $(I_{k\times k}-\sum_{i=1}^p \Phi_i B^i)(\rv_t-\muv)=\av_t$
  • Here, $I_{k\times k}$ is the identity matrix (a diagonal matrix with 1 on the diagonal) and $B$ is the lag operator: $B\rv_t=\rv_{t-1}$
  • $\muv=\begin{pmatrix} \mu_1\\ \vdots\\\mu_k\end{pmatrix}$ is a constant $k$-dimensional vector
  • For $i\in\{1,\dots,p\}$, the AR coefficient matrix $\Phi_i = \begin{bmatrix}\phi_{1,1;i} &\dots & \phi_{1,k;i}\\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ \phi_{k,1;i} &\dots &\phi_{k,k;i}\end{bmatrix}$ is a $k\times k$ constant matrix.

A time series $\{\av_{t}\}$ is a $k$-dimensional weak white noise with mean $\0$ and (instantaneous or contemporaneous) covariance matrix $\Sig$, denoted by $\av_t \sim \text{weak WN}(\0_{k\times 1},\Sig_{k\times k})$, if:

  • $\av_{T}, \av_{T-1}, \dots, \av_1$ are identically distributed
\begin{align*} &\Eb(\av_t)=\0=\begin{pmatrix} 0\\ \vdots\\0\end{pmatrix}_{k\times 1}\\ &\Cov(\av_t,\av_t) = \Eb(\av_t \av_t^\top)=\Sig = \begin{bmatrix}\sig_{1,1} &\dots & \sig_{1,k}\\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ \sig_{k,1} &\dots &\sig_{k,k}\end{bmatrix} \end{align*}
  • For $t\ne s$, the random vectors $\av_t$ and $\av_s$ are uncorrelated
\begin{align*} \Cov(\av_t,\av_s) = \Eb(\av_t \av_s^\top) = \0_{k\times k}=\begin{bmatrix}0 &\dots & 0\\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ 0 &\dots &0\end{bmatrix}_{k\times k}. \end{align*}

2.1. VAR(1) model¶

  • For simplicity, let us only consider 2-dimensional (or bivariate) time series by assuming $k=2$
  • Generalizing to $k\ge3$ is straightforward (though maybe cumbersome to write down)
  • A VAR(1) model is
\begin{align*} \begin{cases} \rv_t - \muv = \Phi (\rv_{t-1}-\muv) + \av_t,\\ \av_t \sim \text{weak WN}(\0_{2\times 1},\Sig_{2\times 2}). \end{cases} \end{align*}
  • Assuming $\rv_t$ is bivariate (i.e. $k=2$), the AR(1) equation has the explicit form
\begin{align*} \begin{pmatrix} r_{t,1}-\mu_1\\ r_{t,2} - \mu_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \phi_{1,1} & \phi_{1,2}\\ \phi_{2,1} & \phi_{2,2} \end{bmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} r_{t-1,1}-\mu_1\\ r_{t-1,2} - \mu_2 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} a_{t,1}\\ a_{t,2} \end{pmatrix} \end{align*}
  • Which, in turn, represents the following equations
\begin{align*} \begin{cases}\displaystyle r_{t,1}-\mu_1 = \phi_{1,1} (r_{t-1,1}-\mu_1) + \phi_{1,2} (r_{t-1,2}-\mu_2) + a_{t,1},\\\\ r_{t,2}-\mu_2 = \phi_{2,1} (r_{t-1,1}-\mu_1) + \phi_{2,2} (r_{t-1,2}-\mu_2) + a_{t,2}, \end{cases} \end{align*}
  • $\phi_{1,1}$ represents the amount of "influence" of $r_{t-1,1}$ on $r_{t,1}$ (in the presence of $r_{t-1,2}$)
  • $\phi_{1,2}$ represents the amount of "influence" of $r_{t-1,2}$ on $r_{t,1}$ (in the presence of $r_{t-1,1}$)
  • Similar interpretations for $\phi_{2,1}$ and $\phi_{2,2}$.
  • Consider the quarterly real gross domestic product (GDP) of Canada and US from 1980-2011
In [8]:
da = read.table("q-ukcaus.txt", header = T)
gdp = ts(da[,4:5], start = c(1980,1), frequency = 4)
plot(gdp)
  • Let us compute the quarterly growth rate of GDP, in percentage
In [9]:
z =diff(log(gdp))*100
plot(z)

  • Next, we check if there is auto- and cross-correlation in the time series.

  • The sample CCM and the multivariate Ljung-Box test indicates there is cross correlation

In [10]:
acf(z)
In [11]:
mq(z, lag = 5)

  • The estimates can be obtained in closed forms.
  • We use the VAR() function of MTS package to fit a VAR(1) model.
  • The fitted model is
\begin{align*} \left(I_{2\times 2} - \begin{bmatrix} 0.268 & 0.461\\ 0.222 & 0.288 \end{bmatrix} B\right) \begin{pmatrix} r_{t,CA} - 0.1559107\\ r_{t,US} - 0.3439829 \end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix} a_{t,CA}\\ a_{t,US} \end{pmatrix} \end{align*}

where

\begin{align*} \begin{pmatrix} a_{t,CA}\\ a_{t,US} \end{pmatrix} \sim \text{weak WN}\left(\begin{pmatrix} 0\\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0.3372501 & 0.1904523\\ 0.1904523 & 0.4273207 \end{bmatrix}\right) \end{align*}

2.2. Granger causality¶

  • Consider the VAR(1) equations
\begin{align*} \begin{cases}\displaystyle r_{t,1}-\mu_1 = \phi_{1,1} (r_{t-1,1}-\mu_1) + \phi_{1,2} (r_{t-1,2}-\mu_2) + a_{t,1},\\\\ r_{t,2}-\mu_2 = \phi_{2,1} (r_{t-1,1}-\mu_1) + \phi_{2,2} (r_{t-1,2}-\mu_2) + a_{t,2}, \end{cases} \end{align*}
  • Assume that $\phi_{2,1}=0$ but $\phi_{1,2}\ne0$
  • Since $\phi_{2,1}=0$, then $r_{t,2}$ is "not influenced" by $r_{t-1,1}$ (see the equation for $r_{t,2}$)
  • However, since $\phi_{1,2}\ne0$, $r_{t,1}$ is influenced by $r_{t-1,2}$
  • If $\phi_{2,1}=0$ but $\phi_{1,2}\ne0$, we say that $r_2=\{r_{t,2}\}$ causes $r_1=\{r_{t,1}\}$
  • This relationship is known as "Granger causality" (with $\rv_2$ causing $\rv_1$)
  • It can be defined for general multivariate time series models.
  • Consider univariate times series $y=\{y_t\}$ and $x=\{x_t\}$
  • We say $x$ causes $y$ if information of $x_{t}, x_{t-2}, \dots$ improves forecasts of $y_{t+h}$
  • Let us check if growth of US GDP causes growth of Canada GDP.
  • We need to test if $\phi_{US, CA}=0$ and $\phi_{CA, US}\ne0$.
  • This can be done by t-ratio tests of the coefficients

2.3. Stationary condition for VAR(1) model¶

  • Consider a VAR(1) model $\rv_t - $ $\muv $ $=$ $\Phi$ $(\rv_{t-1}$ $-\muv) $ $+ \av_t$
  • For any $h>0$, we have
\begin{align*} \rv_t - \muv &= \Phi (\rv_{t-1} - \muv) + \av_t\\ &= \Phi \big(\Phi(\rv_{t-2} - \muv) + \av_{t-1}\big) + \av_t\\ &= \Phi^2 (\rv_{t-2} - \muv) + \av_t + \Phi \av_{t-1}\\ &\vdots\\ &= \Phi^{t-h} (\rv_{t-h} - \muv)+ \sum_{i=0}^{t-h-1} \Phi^i \av_{t-i}. \end{align*}
  • For the moment assume that the times series is defined for all negative values of $t$
  • Then, if $\Phi^{t-h}\to \0_{k\times k}$ as $h\to \infty$, we obtain
\begin{align*} \rv_t - \muv = \lim_{h\to\infty}\left( \Phi^{t-h} (\rv_{t-h} - \muv)+ \sum_{i=0}^{t-h-1} \Phi^i \av_{t-i}\right) = \sum_{i=0}^{\infty} \Phi^i \av_{t-i}. \end{align*}
  • Assuming that the infinite sum on the right hand side is well defined, it will be then clear that $\{r_t\}$ is weakly stationary since $\{\av_t\}$ is assumed to be a weak WN.
  • Thus, $\{\rv_t\}$ is stationary if $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\Phi^n= \0_{k\times k}$

  • Recall the following facts from linear algebra for a matrix $A_{k\times k}$:

    • The eigenvalues of $A$ are the solutions $\lam$ of the determinant equation $\text{det}(\lam I_{k\times k} - A)=0$

    • $A=\0_{k\times k}$ if and only if all its eigenvalues are zero.

    • If $\{\lam_1,\dots,\lam_k\}$ are eigenvalue of $A$, then $\{\lam_1^n,\dots,\lam_k^n\}$ are eigenvalue of $A^n$

  • So, $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\Phi^n= \0_{k\times k}$ if and only if $\lim_{n\to\infty} \lam^n = 0$ for any eigenvalue $\lam$ of $\Phi$
  • It then follows that $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\Phi^n= \0_{k\times k}$ if and only if $|\lam|<1$ for all eigenvalues $\lam$ of $\Phi$
  • Note that the eigenvalues of $\Phi$ are the solutions of $\det(\lam I_{k\times k} - A)=0$
  • The stationary condition for VAR(1) is usually expressed in terms of the solution of the characteristic equation \begin{align*} \det(I_{k\times k} - x \Phi)=0 \end{align*}
  • Since $\det(\lam I_{k\times k} - \Phi)= \lam^k \det\left(I_{k\times k} - \frac{1}{\lam}\Phi\right)$, the (non-zero) eigenvalues of $\Phi$ are the inverse of the solutions of the characteristic equation
  • So, $|\lam|<1$ if and only if $|x|>1$.
  • We obtain the stationary condition of VAR(1) model:
  • VAR(1) is stationary if the absolute values of all the eigenvalues of the AR coefficient matrix $\Phi$ are less one
  • Equivalently, VAR(1) is stationary if all the solutions $x$ of $\det(I_{k\times k} - x \Phi)=0$ satisfy $|x|>1$

  • For $k=1$, these two conditions become the familiar stationary conditions for univariate AR(1) model:

    • AR(1) is stationary if the AR coefficient $\ph$ satisfy $|\ph|<1$

    • The solutions of the characteristic equation $1-\ph x=0$ are outside the unit circle.

  • Let us check if the fitted model for US and Canada is stationary (it should be, otherwise, the estimation method is wrong)
  • First, we find the AR coefficient matrix

3. VAR(2) model¶

  • Consider a VAR(2) model
\begin{align*} \begin{cases} \rv_t - \muv = \Phi_1 (\rv_{t-1}-\muv) + \Phi_2 (\rv_{t-2}-\muv) + \av_t,\\ \av_t \sim \text{weak WN}(\0_{2\times 1},\Sig_{2\times 2}). \end{cases} \end{align*}
  • Assuming $\{\rv_t\}$ is bivariate, the VAR(2) equation is
\begin{align*} \begin{pmatrix} r_{t,1}-\mu_1\\ r_{t,2} - \mu_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \phi_{1,1;1} & \phi_{1,2;1}\\ \phi_{2,1;1} & \phi_{2,2;1} \end{bmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} r_{t-1,1}-\mu_1\\ r_{t-1,2} - \mu_2 \end{pmatrix} +\begin{bmatrix} \phi_{1,1;2} & \phi_{1,2;2}\\ \phi_{2,1;2} & \phi_{2,2;2} \end{bmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} r_{t-1,1}-\mu_1\\ r_{t-1,2} - \mu_2 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} a_{t,1}\\ a_{t,2} \end{pmatrix} \end{align*}
  • Which, in turn, represents the following system of equations
\begin{align*} \begin{cases}\displaystyle r_{t,1}-\mu_1 = \phi_{1,1;1} (r_{t-1,1}-\mu_1) + \phi_{1,2;1} (r_{t-1,2}-\mu_2) + \phi_{1,1;2} (r_{t-2,1}-\mu_1) + \phi_{1,2;2} (r_{t-2,2}-\mu_2) + a_{t,1},\\\\ r_{t,2}-\mu_2 = \phi_{2,1;1} (r_{t-1,1}-\mu_1) + \phi_{2,2;1} (r_{t-1,2}-\mu_2) + \phi_{2,1;2} (r_{t-2,1}-\mu_1) + \phi_{2,2;2} (r_{t-2,2}-\mu_2) + a_{t,2}.\\ \end{cases} \end{align*}
  • $\phi_{1,1;1}$ represents the amount of "influence" of $r_{t-1,1}$ on $r_{t,1}$ (in the presence of $r_{t-1,2}$, $r_{t-2,1}$, and $r_{t-2,2}$)
  • $\phi_{1,1;2}$ represents the amount of "influence" of $r_{t-2,1}$ on $r_{t,1}$ (in the presence of $r_{t-1,1}$, $r_{t-1,2}$, and $r_{t-2,2}$)
  • In general, $\phi_{i,j;h}$ measures the amount of influence of $r_{t-h,j}$ on $r_{t,i}$ in the presence of other lagged values in $\rv_{t-1}$ and $\rv_{t-2}$
  • Let us fit a VAR(2) model to US-Canada GDP growth rates.
  • The fitted model is
\begin{align*} \left(I_{2\times 2} - \begin{bmatrix} 0.320 & 0.520\\ 0.212 & 0.296 \end{bmatrix} B - \begin{bmatrix} -0.118 & -0.0188\\ -0.054 & 0.0588 \end{bmatrix} B^2 \right) \begin{pmatrix} r_{t,CA} - 0.1620669\\ r_{t,US} - 0.3391791 \end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix} a_{t,CA}\\ a_{t,US} \end{pmatrix} \end{align*}

where

\begin{align*} \begin{pmatrix} a_{t,CA}\\ a_{t,US} \end{pmatrix} \sim \text{weak WN}\left(\begin{pmatrix} 0\\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0.3270977 & 0.1899463\\ 0.1899463 & 0.4293033 \end{bmatrix}\right) \end{align*}

3.1. VAR(1) representation of VAR(2) model¶

  • VAR(2) model can be seen as a higher dimensional VAR(1) model.
  • For example, a 2 dimensional AR(2) process can be seen as a 4 dimensional AR(1) process.
  • We show this next. First, define a new time series $\{\xv_t\}$ by stacking $\rv_{t}-\muv$ on top of $\rv_{t-1}-\muv$:
\begin{align*} \xv_t = \vec([\rv_t-\muv, \rv_{t-1}-\muv]) =\begin{pmatrix}r_{t,1}-\mu_1\\ r_{t,2}-\mu_2\\ r_{t-1,1}-\mu_1\\ r_{t-1,2}-\mu_2\end{pmatrix} \end{align*}
  • We then have
\begin{align*} \xv_t &= \begin{pmatrix}\rv_t-\muv\\ \rv_{t-1}-\muv\end{pmatrix}\\\\ &= \begin{pmatrix} \Phi_1 (\rv_{t-1}-\muv) + \Phi_2 (\rv_{t-2}-\muv) + \av_t\\ I_{k\times k} (\rv_{t-1}-\muv) + \0_{k\times k} (\rv_{t-2}-\muv)\end{pmatrix}\\\\ &= \begin{bmatrix} \Phi_1 & \Phi_2 \\ I_{k\times k} & \0_{k\times k}\end{bmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\rv_{t-1}-\muv\\ \rv_{t-2}-\muv\end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix}\av_t\\ \0_{k\times 1}\end{pmatrix} \end{align*}
  • Note that $\begin{pmatrix}\rv_{t-1}-\muv\\ \rv_{t-2}-\muv\end{pmatrix}$ $=$ $\xv_{t-1}$
  • Let us also define $\bv_t := \begin{pmatrix}\av_t\\ \0_{k\times 1}\end{pmatrix}$ and $\Phiv$ $ := $ $\begin{bmatrix} \Phi_1 & \Phi_2 \\ I_{k\times k} & \0_{k\times k}\end{bmatrix}$

  • We then have $\xv_t = \Phiv \xv_{t-1} + \bv_t$.

  • So, the $2k$ dimensional time series $\{\xv_t\}$ has a VAR(1) model.

  • The matrix $\Phiv := \begin{bmatrix} \Phi_1 & \Phi_2 \\ I_{k\times k} & \0_{k\times k}\end{bmatrix}$ is called the companion Matrix of the VAR(2) model.
  • For a VAR model fitted with VAR() function of MTS package, you can get the top blocks of the companion matrix by using $Phi

3.2. Stationary conditions of VAR(2) model¶

  • The stationary condition of VAR(2) model follows from its VAR(1) representation
  • VAR(2) is stationary if all the eigenvalues of the companion matrix $\Phiv := \begin{bmatrix} \Phi_1 & \Phi_2 \\ I_{k\times k} & \0_{k\times k}\end{bmatrix}$ have absolute value less than 1.
  • With a little more work, we can derive a more familiar condition.
  • The characteristic equation of the VAR(1) representation is
\begin{align*} 0&=\det\left(I_{2k\times 2k} - x \Phi\right)\\ &=\det\left(\begin{bmatrix} I_{k\times k} & \0_{k\times k}\\ \0_{k\times k} & I_{k\times k} \end{bmatrix} - x \begin{bmatrix} \Phi_1 & \Phi_2 \\ I_{k\times k} & \0_{k\times k}\end{bmatrix}\right)\\ &=\det\left(\begin{bmatrix} I_{k\times k}- x \Phi_1 & - x \Phi_2 \\ -x I_{k\times k} & I_{k\times k}\end{bmatrix}\right)\\ &=\det\left(I_{k\times k} - x \Phi_1 - x^2 \Phi_2 \right) \end{align*}
  • In the last step, we used the following formula for determinant of a block matrix. If $CD=DC$, then
\begin{align*} \det\left(\begin{bmatrix} A_{k\times k} & B_{k\times k}\\ C_{k\times k} & D_{k\times k} \end{bmatrix}\right) = \det\left( A D - B C\right) \end{align*}
  • Finally, we obtain that the alternative stationary condition for VAR(2) process. It is stationary if all the solutions x of the following determinant equation satisfy $|x|>1$ \begin{align*} \det\left(I_{k\times k} - x \Phi_1 - x^2 \Phi_2 \right)=0. \end{align*}
  • Compare this condition with the stationary condition of the AR(2) model. Recall the condition: the solutions of $1-\phi_1 x- \phi_2 x^2=0$ has absolute value greater than 1.
  • Let us check if the fitted VAR(2) model of the US-Canada GDP growth rates is stationary
  • We can apply the eigen() function to the companion matrix.
  • First, we need to find the companion matrix. The top blocks are stored in $Phi of a fitted model with VAR() function.
  • We only need to add $[I_{k\times k}, \0_{k\times k}]$ below it.

4. VAR(p) model¶

  • The general case if VAR(p) model is
\begin{align*} \begin{cases} \rv_t - \muv = \sum_{i=1}^p \Phi_i (\rv_{t-i}-\muv) + \av_t\\\\ \av_t \sim \text{weak WN}(\0_{k\times 1},\Sig_{k\times k}) \end{cases}\quad\quad\text{or }\quad \begin{cases} (I_{k\times k}-\sum_{i=1}^p \Phi_i B)(\rv_t-\muv)=\av_t\\\\ \av_t \sim \text{weak WN}(\0_{k\times 1},\Sig_{k\times k}) \end{cases} \end{align*}
  • This model is estimated using GLS or MLE.
  • Define
\begin{align*} \xv_t &=\vec([\rv_t-\muv,\dots,\rv_{t-p+1}-\muv])\\ \bv_t &=\vec([\av_t,\underbrace{\0_{k\times 1},\dots,\0_{k\times 1}}_{p-1 \text{ times }}])=\begin{pmatrix}\av_t\\ \0_{k(p-1)\times 1}\end{pmatrix} \end{align*}
  • Define, also, the "companion matrix"
\begin{align*} \Phiv := \begin{bmatrix} \Phi_1 \dots \Phi_{p-1} & \Phi_p \\ I_{k(p-1)\times k(p-1)} & \0_{k(p-1)\times k}\end{bmatrix} \end{align*}
  • The VAR(1) representation of VAR(p) is $\xv_t = \Phiv \xv_{t-1} + \bv_t$
  • A $k-$dimensional VAR(p) model has a $pk$ dimensional VAR(1) representation
  • VAR(p) is stationary if all the eigenvalues of the companion matrix $\Phiv$ are in the unit circle (i.e. $|\lam|<1$)
  • Equivalently, Var(p) is stationary if its characteristic equation, defined below, does not have a unit root (i.e. $|x|>1$ for all solutions $x$) \begin{align*} \det\left(I_{k\times k} - \sum_{i=1}^p x^i \,\Phi_i \right)=0. \end{align*}

4.1. VAR order selection¶

  • Several procedures have been suggested for selecting the order $p$ of a VAR(p) model

  • They generally fall into one of the following two categories:

    1. Sequential likelihood-ratio tests: These methods work similar to an ANOVA table for multiple regression. Roughly speaking, we start with a high value for $p$ and keep reducing the number $p$ until the reduced model is significant.

    2. Information criteria: This should be fairly straight forward to understand. Select a model that minimizes BIC or AIC.

  • You can use the VARorder() function of the MTS package to perform VAR order selection
  • It reports the $p$ that minimizes three Information Criterion, namely, AIC, BIC, and HQ (Hannan-Quinn). It also output the so-called M-statistic which is a likelihood ration test statistic.
  • BIC and HQ indicate $p=1$. AIC indicate $p=3$. M-stat indicates $p=2$ under 5% test level.

4.2. Model checking¶

  • To check that the VAR(p) model is adequate, we should check its assumptions
  • Specifically, we should check that the residuals are multi-dimensional weak WN
  • This can be done through sample CCM and multivariate Ljung-Box test.
  • The degree of freedom of the Ljung-Box test must be corrected by the number of AR parameters of the VAR(p) model (i.e. $kp$)
  • Use the MTSdiag() function in the MTS package to perform model testing
  • The output uses the simplified CCM: "$\cdot$" indicates insignificant correlation, "+" is significant positive correlation and "-" is significant negative correlation.
  • We can see that the residuals are weak WN and the VAR(1) model is adequate.
